name: Venetian Yellow
lede: Venetian Yellow is a moderate yellow that Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary traces to about 1874, and in our archive it is disproportionately a color of Kalighat painting from Bengal, not of Venice.

sections.title: An 1874 entry, renamed again in 1924
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's *A Dictionary of Color* (1930) gives this hue at plate 10, position J 3, first recorded around 1874 [1]. The same catalogue later listed a second name, Snapdragon, at the neighboring position J 4 in 1924, so the plate held two yellow entries fifty years apart [1]. Our library classes "Venetian" as a place-or-institution word, and nothing in our sources explains why this particular yellow carries it [2].

Its closest named relatives are [[sunbeam]], 2.5 units away and duller, and [[orpiment]], a touch more vivid at 3.4 units, named for the mineral pigment rather than a place [3].

Further out are [[mustard-yellow]], almost the same at 4 units, and [[gamboge-yellow]], more vivid at 4.4, named for a different pigment entirely [3]. Our library files the name under fashion and textiles rather than nature or pigment, a classification worth keeping in mind before assuming any link to actual Venetian paint practice [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Venetian Yellow is common in our archive of 23,781 paintings: a color within six units of it covers at least five per cent of a canvas in 256 works, as photographed [4]. It is strikingly overrepresented in Kalighat painting, at nearly 36 times the archive's overall rate, and in works from India generally, at over six times the rate [4]. Kishi Ganku's 1801 *Bamboo* carries it across three-quarters of the canvas [4]. It most often shares a canvas with other yellows, mustard and khaki [4]. These are screen colors read from photographs of varnished paintings, not pigment tests [4]. By decade, it peaks in the 1820s, in 30 of 731 paintings, at nearly four times the archive's overall rate [4]. George Dawe, a portraitist, also carries it well above the archive rate, at over seven times the expected level [4].
